tagline: The shortest and fastest of the four Gospels: the story of Jesus, the Son of God, who came to serve and to give his life, told at a run toward the cross and an empty tomb.
overview:
Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, the books that tell the story of Jesus' ministry, death, and resurrection. It opens with a single line that works as a title, “This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1), and then moves at speed. There is no birth story and no long sermon like Matthew's Sermon on the Mount. John the Baptist appears in the wilderness, Jesus is baptized and tested, and within a few verses he is in Galilee calling fishermen, casting out unclean spirits, healing the sick, forgiving sins, and colliding with the religious authorities.

The book turns on a question: who is this man? Crowds, demons, disciples, and opponents all try to answer it. Halfway through, at Caesarea Philippi, Peter says, “You are the Christ” (8:29), and at once Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed, and rise again (8:31). From there the story walks the road to Jerusalem, where Jesus enters the city, confronts the temple, is arrested, tried, and crucified. The first human being in Mark to call him the Son of God is a Roman centurion at the foot of the cross, at the moment of his death (15:39). The book closes with women at an empty tomb, told that he has risen.

Mark matters because most scholars judge it the earliest written Gospel, and because it refuses to separate who Jesus is from what he suffered. Its Jesus has authority over storms, disease, and demons, and he uses that authority on the way to a cross. The sentence many readers take as the book's center says it plainly: “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (10:45).
author:
Like the other Gospels, Mark does not name its author in the text. The title According to Mark was attached in the early church, and the tradition behind it is early. Papias, a bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor writing in the early second century, is reported by the church historian Eusebius (in his Ecclesiastical History, 3.39) to have said, on the authority of an older teacher he calls the elder, that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately, though not in order, what he remembered of the things the Lord said and did. Later writers, including Irenaeus near the end of the second century, repeat and expand the link between Mark and Peter.

The Mark of this tradition is usually identified with John Mark of the New Testament: the son of a Mary whose Jerusalem house was a meeting place for the church (Acts 12:12), a companion of Paul and Barnabas who turned back partway through their first mission trip (Acts 13:13), the cause of a sharp split between them (Acts 15:37-39), and later a trusted coworker of Paul (Colossians 4:10, 2 Timothy 4:11). First Peter 5:13 sends greetings from “my son Mark,” which fits the Petrine link. Many scholars accept the tradition in broad terms; Richard Bauckham, in Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (2006), argued at length that Mark rests on Peter's testimony. Others doubt that Papias knew what he claimed, or think the name Mark was common enough that the identification with John Mark is uncertain; Michael Kok (The Gospel on the Margins, 2015) argues that the Petrine link was drawn in the second century partly to secure a little-read Gospel's standing. What nearly everyone agrees on is that the author wrote in plain, vivid Greek, knew Aramaic (he keeps Aramaic phrases and translates them), and wrote for readers who needed Jewish customs explained.
date:
Most scholars date Mark between the late 60s and the early 70s AD, and the debate within that range turns largely on chapter 13, where Jesus predicts the destruction of the temple. Some read the chapter as written during the Jewish revolt against Rome (AD 66-70), when the temple was threatened but still standing, and note that it does not describe the city's fall in the kind of detail one might expect after the event. Others place it just after AD 70, holding that the destruction stands behind the text. Scholars who take Jesus' prophecy as genuine predictive speech see no need to date the book after the event on that ground.

The early tradition is divided: Irenaeus placed the writing after the deaths of Peter and Paul, which tradition sets in Rome under Nero in the mid 60s, while Clement of Alexandria said Mark wrote while Peter was still preaching in Rome. A minority of scholars argues for a considerably earlier date, in the 40s or 50s.

Mark's date is tied to the question of how the first three Gospels (the Synoptics, so called because they can be seen together) relate. Most scholars today hold that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, since they reproduce most of its content and often its wording and order. A minority defends other views: some, following the church tradition that goes back to Augustine, hold that Matthew came first, and the Two-Gospel hypothesis, revived by William Farmer in the 1960s, holds that Mark drew on both Matthew and Luke. On the majority view, Mark's date also shapes the dating of Matthew and Luke.
setting:
Jesus' ministry took place in the late 20s or early 30s AD, in a land ruled by Rome. Galilee in the north was governed by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, while Judea and Jerusalem were under a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, from about AD 26 to 36. The Jerusalem temple, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great, was the center of Jewish worship and was run by the high priest and the chief priestly families, who answered to Rome. Pharisees (a lay renewal movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and its traditions), scribes (experts in the law), and Sadducees (the priestly aristocracy) all appear as Jesus' questioners and opponents.

Mark's first readers are less certain. The tradition places them in Rome, and the book has features that fit: it explains Jewish washing customs (7:3-4), translates Aramaic words, and uses several Latin loanwords, including one that explains a Jewish coin in terms of Roman money (12:42). Its steady attention to suffering and to faithfulness under pressure would have spoken directly to Christians in Rome after Nero's persecution following the great fire of AD 64. Other scholars propose Syria or Galilee as the setting. On any view the readers were largely Gentile believers who needed to understand both the Jewish world of Jesus and the cost of following him.
purpose: Mark calls his book a gospel, meaning good news, and in the Roman world that word could announce a victory or the accession of an emperor. Mark uses it for the news that God's kingdom has come near in Jesus (1:14-15). The book is written to tell who Jesus is, the Christ and the Son of God, and to show that his identity cannot be understood apart from the cross. It also shapes disciples. The Twelve in Mark are slow, frightened, and often wrong, and the book presents their failures honestly, which would have both warned and comforted readers who were themselves being tested. Jesus' call to deny oneself, take up the cross, and follow (8:34) is addressed to every reader, not only to the first followers.
story: Mark picks up the story where the Old Testament's prophets left it. It begins with a quotation from Isaiah and Malachi about a messenger preparing the way of the Lord, so that John the Baptist steps into Israel's long hope for God's return and the renewal of his people. Jesus then announces that the time is fulfilled. The book ends at the empty tomb with a promise that the risen Jesus is going ahead of his disciples into Galilee, which points forward to the church's witness in Acts and the letters. Matthew and Luke retell much of Mark's account with material of their own, and John tells the same story from a different angle.
christ: Mark is entirely about Christ, and it builds its portrait from two sides. On one side is authority: Jesus forgives sins, which his opponents say only God can do (2:7), calms the sea, raises a dead girl, and speaks with the authority of Israel's God. On the other is suffering: three times he predicts his death and resurrection (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34), and each time the disciples misunderstand. Mark holds these together. The Son of God is recognized fully only at the cross, and Jesus' usual name for himself, the Son of Man, draws on Daniel 7's figure who receives everlasting dominion while also being the one who gives his life as a ransom. The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners and bodily raised.
reading:
Read Mark in one sitting if you can; it takes about as long as a film, and its force comes from its pace. Watch the word translated “immediately,” which appears more than forty times and drives the action forward. Notice Mark's habit of sandwiching one story inside another (for example, Jairus's daughter and the bleeding woman in chapter 5), where each story explains the other. Watch the commands to silence, where Jesus tells people and demons not to make him known; since William Wrede's study of 1901 this has been called the messianic secret, and interpreters still debate what it means. Most readers see it as Jesus' refusal to be taken for the wrong kind of messiah before the cross made his meaning clear.

The ending needs a note. The oldest complete Greek manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus from the fourth century, end the book at 16:8, with the women fleeing from the tomb in fear. Most later manuscripts include 16:9-20, the longer ending, and it was known by the late second century, since Irenaeus cites it. One Old Latin manuscript has a brief shorter ending instead, and several Greek manuscripts carry both. Most scholars conclude that 16:9-20 was added early by another hand, drawing on material found in the other Gospels and Acts; a minority defends it as original. Among those who think it was added, some hold that Mark meant to end at 16:8, leaving the reader with the promise of Galilee and the silence of the women, while others think the original ending was lost. Most modern Bibles print the longer ending with a note, and readers can treat it with the care that the evidence calls for.
text:
Mark was copied less than the other Gospels in the early centuries, and it has fewer early witnesses. The oldest is a small papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, P137 (P.Oxy. 5345), with a few words of 1:7-9 and 1:16-18, published in 2018 and dated to the late second or early third century; it is the fragment once rumored to be a first-century copy of Mark, a date its editors did not confirm. The Chester Beatty papyrus P45, from the third century and now in Dublin, preserves parts of Mark 4 to 9 and 11 to 12 in a codex that once held all four Gospels and Acts. The complete text comes first from the fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, then from the fifth-century Alexandrinus, Bezae, and Washingtonianus (W, in the Freer Gallery in Washington, whose text of Mark is unusually mixed), and from early Latin, Syriac, and Coptic translations.

Four places in Mark are where English Bibles most visibly part company. At 1:1 some early witnesses lack ‘the Son of God’. At 1:2 the earliest manuscripts attribute a combined quotation to ‘Isaiah the prophet’, while later ones, followed by the King James Version, read ‘the prophets’. At 1:41 most manuscripts say Jesus was moved with compassion and a few say he was angry. The largest question is the ending. Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8, and Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Questions to Marinus in the early fourth century, reported that the accurate copies, nearly all of them, ended there. Most later manuscripts carry 16:9-20. The Old Latin Codex Bobiensis (k), of the late fourth or early fifth century, alone ends with a brief shorter ending after 16:8; several Greek manuscripts have both endings; and Codex W inserts a further saying of the risen Jesus after 16:14, known as the Freer Logion. The King James Version, translated from the Textus Receptus, prints 16:9-20 without comment; modern versions print it with a note or in brackets.

A different kind of textual question was raised in 1958, when Morton Smith photographed at the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem an eighteenth-century copy of a letter attributed to Clement of Alexandria, which quotes from a longer, secret edition of Mark kept in Alexandria. Smith published it in 1973. Its authenticity is disputed: Stephen Carlson (The Gospel Hoax, 2005) argued that Smith forged it, while others defend it as a genuine ancient letter. No manuscript of Mark contains the passages it quotes, and no English Bible prints them.
reception:
For most of the church's history Mark was the least read of the Gospels. Papias, as Eusebius reports him (Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15), defended the book as Peter's teaching set down by his interpreter, but also conceded that it was not written in order, which suggests it already needed defending. Hippolytus of Rome, in the early third century, called Mark ‘stump-fingered’ in his Refutation of All Heresies (book 7), a nickname repeated in the old Latin prologue to the Gospel. Augustine, in his Harmony of the Gospels (1.2.4, around 400), called Mark the follower and abbreviator of Matthew, and though he later allowed that Mark drew on Luke as well, the judgment stuck: if nearly all of Mark was in Matthew, a reader lost little by skipping it. The results show in the commentaries. The Greek catena on Mark attributed to Victor of Antioch, compiled around 500, had to be assembled largely from comments on the other Gospels, because there was no commentary tradition on Mark to draw on. Jerome preached a series of homilies on passages of Mark at Bethlehem in the first decade of the fifth century. The earliest surviving full commentary is the Latin Exposition of Mark written by the Irish monk Cummian around 610, long circulated under Jerome's name, and Bede of Jarrow wrote another in the early eighth century. In Greek, Theophylact of Ohrid wrote a continuous exposition in the late eleventh century. Brenda Deen Schildgen (Power and Prejudice, 1999) and Michael Kok (The Gospel on the Margins, 2015) have traced this long neglect in detail.

Mark's place in Christian imagination came less through commentary than through symbol and place. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 3.11.8, around 180) matched the four Gospels to the four living creatures of Revelation 4:7 and gave Mark the eagle, because he begins with the prophetic Spirit coming down from on high; he gave John the lion. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 1.6) gave Mark the man. The scheme that prevailed was Jerome's, in the preface to his Commentary on Matthew (398): Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle, with Mark the lion because his Gospel opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness. Jerome's lion marks Mark in the Book of Kells and on countless pulpits. Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 2.16) records that Mark was the first to preach in Egypt and founded the churches of Alexandria, and the Coptic Orthodox Church still calls its patriarch the successor of Mark. In 828 two Venetian merchants carried relics said to be Mark's from Alexandria to Venice, which built the basilica of San Marco to house them and flew the winged lion as the emblem of the republic; Tintoretto's Miracle of the Slave (1548) shows the saint plunging from heaven to rescue a Venetian servant.

The nineteenth century turned the neglected Gospel into the most studied one. Karl Lachmann (1835) observed that Matthew and Luke agree in order only when they agree with Mark, and in 1838 Christian Gottlob Wilke and Christian Hermann Weisse independently concluded that Mark was the source both used. Heinrich Julius Holtzmann's Die synoptischen Evangelien (1863) made the view standard in Germany, and Mark became the backbone of the liberal Lives of Jesus, prized as the plainest, least theological account. Two books undid that picture. Martin Kähler (1892) called the Gospels passion narratives with extended introductions, and William Wrede's study of the messianic secret (1901) argued that Mark was theology through and through. Karl Ludwig Schmidt (1919) and Rudolf Bultmann (1921) treated Mark as a string of once-separate traditions; Willi Marxsen (Der Evangelist Markus, 1956) founded redaction criticism by reading Mark as an author with a theology of his own; David Rhoads and Donald Michie (Mark as Story, 1982) led the turn to reading it as a unified narrative; and Ched Myers (Binding the Strong Man, 1988) offered a political reading from the Catholic Worker tradition. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) revived the case for Peter's testimony, and Joel Marcus and Adela Yarbro Collins have written the fullest modern commentaries on its Jewish and Greco-Roman setting. Jewish scholars have read Mark as a Jewish text: Lawrence Wills annotated it for The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2011).

In worship Mark came into its own only recently. The Roman Catholic lectionary of 1969, with its three-year cycle, gave Mark its own year (Year B), and the Revised Common Lectionary (1992), used by many Protestant churches, follows the same pattern, supplementing Mark's short text with John 6 in the summer. Mark's passion narrative is read on Palm Sunday in that year. The Gospel's brevity and pace also made it the one most often performed whole: the English actor Alec McCowen recited it from memory in the King James Version on the London stage and then on Broadway in 1978, and many churches have since followed him in reading it aloud in a single sitting.

structure.title: The beginning of the gospel
structure.summary: Framed by the word gospel (1:1 and 1:14-15), the prologue tells the reader who Jesus is before any character knows: John prepares the way, Jesus is baptized and named Son by the Father's voice, is driven into the wilderness, and then announces that the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God has come near.

structure.title: Authority in Galilee
structure.summary: The section opens beside the sea with the call of four fishermen (1:16-20). Jesus teaches with authority, casts out spirits, heals, and forgives sins, and a chain of five controversies (2:1-3:6) ends with Pharisees and Herodians plotting to destroy him.

structure.title: Parables, power, and rejection
structure.summary: Opening with a summary by the sea (3:7-12) and the appointment of the Twelve (3:13-19), the section sets Jesus' new family against misunderstanding relatives and hostile scribes, teaches in parables, shows authority over sea, demons, disease, and death, and closes with his rejection at Nazareth (6:1-6).

structure.title: Bread and blindness
structure.summary: Like the two before it, this section begins with the disciples, now sent out two by two (6:7-13). John is executed, Jesus feeds great crowds twice and walks on the sea, and the section ends with the disciples still failing to understand about the loaves (8:14-21) and a blind man healed in two stages (8:22-26).

structure.title: On the way to the cross
structure.summary: Mark marks this section with the phrase on the way (8:27, 9:33-34, 10:32, 10:52). Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and on the road to Jerusalem Jesus three times predicts his death and resurrection and each time teaches what following him costs. A blind man healed at Jericho, who follows him on the way, closes the section.

structure.title: Jesus in Jerusalem
structure.summary: From the approach to the city (11:1), Mark counts the days (11:11, 11:12, 11:20). Jesus enters Jerusalem, clears the temple, debates the authorities, and on the Mount of Olives foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man.

structure.title: The passion
structure.summary: Opening with the note that the Passover was two days away (14:1), and then marked by hours (15:1, 15:25, 15:33-34, 15:42), the passion tells of the anointing, the last meal, Gethsemane, the betrayal, the trials, Peter's denial, the crucifixion, and the burial.

structure.title: The empty tomb
structure.summary: The women find the tomb open and hear that Jesus has risen and is going ahead of the disciples into Galilee; they flee, saying nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. Here the oldest complete manuscripts end.

structure.title: The longer ending
structure.summary: A summary of resurrection appearances, the commission, and the ascension, found in most later manuscripts and known by the late second century but absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus; most modern Bibles print it with a note.

themes.title: The kingdom of God has come near
themes.body: Jesus' first words in Mark announce that the time is fulfilled and God's kingdom is near (1:15). The kingdom is God's reign breaking into a world held by sickness, evil spirits, and sin. Jesus' healings and exorcisms are signs of that reign, and his parables in chapter 4 explain that it grows from hidden, small beginnings to a great harvest.

themes.title: Who is this man?
themes.body: The question of Jesus' identity runs through the whole book. The disciples ask it after the storm (4:41), Herod wonders about it, and Jesus asks it himself at Caesarea Philippi (8:29). The reader knows the answer from 1:1, and the drama lies in watching the characters struggle toward it, often getting the words right and the meaning wrong.

themes.title: The way of the cross
themes.body: After Peter's confession, every prediction of the passion is followed by teaching on discipleship: deny yourself, be the servant of all, and follow Jesus to the cross. Mark insists that the Messiah's path runs through suffering and that his followers' path does too. This was not abstract for readers who faced persecution.

themes.title: Failure and grace
themes.body: Mark does not flatter the disciples. They misunderstand, argue about greatness, fall asleep in Gethsemane, and flee at the arrest, and Peter denies Jesus three times. Yet the angel's message at the tomb names Peter in particular (16:7). The book offers hope not in the disciples' strength but in the faithfulness of the one who goes ahead of them.

keyChapters.why: The title verse, John's preaching, Jesus' baptism, and the announcement of the kingdom set the terms for the whole book.
The parables of the kingdom and the stilling of the storm show how God's reign grows and raise the question of who Jesus is.
Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi and the first passion prediction are the hinge of the Gospel.
Jesus teaches the way of the servant and gives the book's central statement of why he came, to give his life as a ransom for many.
The Olivet discourse foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man and calls disciples to watchfulness.
The crucifixion, where the centurion confesses Jesus as the Son of God, is the climax of Mark's portrait.
The empty tomb and the message of the resurrection close the book, and the question of its ending is best understood here.

furtherReading.author: N. T. Wright
furtherReading.title: Mark for Everyone
furtherReading.note: Short passages with Wright's own translation and brief, historically informed reflections; an easy first companion.

furtherReading.author: Donald English
furtherReading.title: The Message of Mark
furtherReading.note: A warm, nontechnical Methodist exposition that follows Mark's story and its call to discipleship.

furtherReading.author: Timothy Keller
furtherReading.title: King's Cross: The Story of the World in the Life of Jesus
furtherReading.note: Sermons on Mark by a Presbyterian pastor, written for skeptics and new readers as much as for believers.

furtherReading.author: William L. Lane
furtherReading.title: The Gospel according to Mark
furtherReading.series: New International Commentary on the New Testament
furtherReading.note: An evangelical classic that reads Mark as a book for a persecuted church in Nero's Rome.

furtherReading.author: James R. Edwards
furtherReading.title: The Gospel according to Mark
furtherReading.note: Clear and theologically rich, with a sharp eye for Mark's sandwiches, irony, and literary design.

furtherReading.author: R. T. France
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Mark
furtherReading.note: A careful commentary on the Greek text, judicious on history and structure; the best single volume for a preacher who reads Greek.

furtherReading.author: Morna D. Hooker
furtherReading.title: The Gospel according to Saint Mark
furtherReading.note: A concise, balanced commentary by a Methodist scholar at Cambridge, based on her own translation.

furtherReading.author: John R. Donahue and Daniel J. Harrington
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Mark
furtherReading.note: A Roman Catholic commentary attentive to Mark's use of the Old Testament and its literary patterns.

furtherReading.author: Thomas C. Oden and Christopher A. Hall, editors
furtherReading.title: Mark
furtherReading.note: Selections from the church fathers arranged passage by passage, showing how the early church read Mark.

furtherReading.author: Joel Marcus
furtherReading.title: Mark 1-8
furtherReading.note: A learned commentary, followed by Mark 8-16 (2009), especially strong on Jewish background and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

furtherReading.author: Adela Yarbro Collins
furtherReading.title: Mark: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: The fullest critical commentary, placing Mark among ancient Jewish and Greco-Roman writings.

furtherReading.author: Robert H. Gundry
furtherReading.title: Mark: A Commentary on His Apology for the Cross
furtherReading.note: A massive evangelical commentary arguing that Mark was written to answer the scandal of a crucified Messiah.

furtherReading.author: Ched Myers
furtherReading.title: Binding the Strong Man: A Political Reading of Mark's Story of Jesus
furtherReading.note: An influential socio-political reading from the Catholic Worker and radical discipleship tradition.

furtherReading.author: Michael J. Kok
furtherReading.title: The Gospel on the Margins: The Reception of Mark in the Second Century
furtherReading.note: A study of why Mark was so little read in the early church and how the tradition of its link to Peter arose.

furtherReading.author: Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler, editors
furtherReading.title: The Jewish Annotated New Testament
furtherReading.note: Jewish scholars annotate the New Testament; Lawrence Wills's notes on Mark explain its Jewish setting (second edition 2017).
